title: "7. Propensity score and weights"

This script compares the two groups at baseline, fits the propensity score model and computes the inverse probability of treatment weights. It adds `propensity_score` and `ipw` to `patients` for [8. Outcomes](08_outcomes.qmd).

::: {.Rcode title="Source code"}
The full R script is available at:

-   [`R/07_propensity.R`](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Harris-Health-STR/blob/main/R/07_propensity.R)

This R script file is itself reliant on the following helper files:

-   [`R/setup.R`](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Harris-Health-STR/blob/main/R/setup.R)
-   [`R/functions.R`](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Harris-Health-STR/blob/main/R/functions.R)

Translated from [`stata/Do Final Analysis.do`](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Harris-Health-STR/blob/main/stata/Do%20Final%20Analysis.do), lines 70-127.

The code sections below are imported directly from that script when this page is rendered.
:::

## Propensity model

The covariates are those listed in the paper. In Stata, `Gender` was the numbered category made by `encode` (1 = F, 2 = M) entered as a number, which is the same model as a male indicator. Patients missing any covariate, for example with no viral load before ART, get no score and so no weight, and drop out of the weighted analyses, as they did in Stata.

One difference to know about: if a category predicts the regimen perfectly (every patient in it started the STR, say), Stata's `logistic` drops that category and its patients with a note, while `glm()` keeps them and gives probabilities close to 0 or 1, and so very large weights. Check the fitted model for this before using the weights.

```{r}
#| label: fit-propensity-model
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: asis
stata_for("fit-propensity-model")
```

## Weights

Stata:

```stata
predict PropensityScore, p
generate IPW=(InitialRegimenSTR/PropensityScore)+(1-InitialRegimenSTR)/(1-PropensityScore)
```

The formula picks 1/p for STR patients and 1/(1-p) for the others; `if_else()` says so directly. These are average-treatment-effect weights.

```{r}
#| label: compute-weights
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: asis
stata_for("compute-weights")
```

## Weighted balance

Stata repeated the baseline tables with `[aw=IPW]`. Weighted means and proportions by group show whether weighting balanced the covariates; standardised differences are the usual summary.

```{r}
#| label: check-weighted-balance
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: asis
stata_for("check-weighted-balance")
```

## Weighted balance by category

Stata also ran `tab InitialRegimenSTR <variable> [aw=IPW], row` for ethnicity, risk factor, age group, baseline viral load and CD4 groups, and insurance (lines 116-117 and 124-127). A loop over the variable names applies [`weighted_distribution()`](functions.qmd#weighted-category-distributions) to each and stacks the results into one table, so the whole distribution can be compared between groups, not just the means.

```{r}
#| label: check-weighted-category-balance
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: asis
stata_for("check-weighted-category-balance")
```
